outputs.L1: An apparatus and method for latching one pole contact of at least one springy pole in a relay or hybrid switch, for maintaining either an engaged or disengaged state of at least one first contact with said pole contact by means of a mechanical latching device. The mechanical latching device comprises a springy lock pin exerting a minute force, a slider having an indentation path for guiding the lock pin, and a track for the slider. The latching device extends from an armature or the springy pole to a base or body of the relay or hybrid switch. The springy pole is guided by movement of the slider, propelled either by a pull generated by a voltage-rated magnetic coil fed by a pulse of said rated voltage, or by a push exerted by a plunger. For operating a stronger coil to switch higher electrical current, the magnetic coil is fed in combination with at least one higher-voltage discharge to increase the magnetic pulling power of the coil.
outputs.L2: A device and method are provided for mechanically latching a pole contact of at least one resilient pole in either a relay or a hybrid switch, so that at least one first contact is held in either an engaged or disengaged condition with the pole contact. The mechanical latch includes a flexible locking pin that applies only a very small force, a slider having an indented guide path for directing the locking pin, and a track along which the slider moves. The latching mechanism is arranged between an armature or the resilient pole and a base or housing of the relay or hybrid switch. Movement of the resilient pole is controlled by the slider, which is driven either by pulling action from a voltage-rated magnetic coil energized by a pulse of its rated voltage, or by pushing action from a plunger. When a stronger coil is required for switching a higher electrical current, the magnetic coil is supplied in combination with at least one higher-voltage discharge to increase the coil’s magnetic pulling force.
outputs.L3:
The apparatus and method provide a mechanical latching arrangement for a relay or hybrid switch that holds a pole contact in a selected contact state. In particular, the latching arrangement is configured to maintain the pole contact either in an engaged state, in which the contact is closed, or in a disengaged state, in which the contact is open. By mechanically retaining the selected state, the relay or hybrid switch can remain in position without requiring continuous energization of an actuator coil.

The mechanical latching device includes a springy lock pin, a slider, and a track that guides movement of the slider. The slider is formed with an indentation path that cooperates with the springy lock pin. As the slider moves along the track, the lock pin follows the indentation path and is selectively retained at defined positions. These retained positions correspond to the engaged and disengaged states of the pole contact, thereby allowing the latching device to hold the relay or hybrid switch in its selected operating condition.

The latching device extends between the armature or springy pole and the base or body of the relay or hybrid switch. In this configuration, movement of the slider is mechanically coupled to the movement of the pole. The springy pole is therefore guided and positioned by the slider as the slider travels along the track. Depending on the design, the slider may be driven by a magnetic coil that receives a rated-voltage pulse, or it may be moved by a plunger. In either case, the slider movement causes the pole contact to transition between its engaged and disengaged states, after which the lock pin and indentation path maintain the selected position.

For applications requiring switching of higher electrical current, the apparatus may employ a stronger magnetic coil to provide increased actuation force. This stronger coil can be operated using a rated-voltage feed in combination with at least one higher-voltage discharge. The higher-voltage discharge temporarily increases the magnetic pull power of the coil, enabling reliable movement of the armature, pole, or slider under higher load conditions. Once the switching operation is completed, the mechanical latch maintains the contact state without the need for sustained high-power coil operation.
outputs.L4:
A relay or hybrid switch can be designed to hold its electrical contacts in either an engaged or disengaged state by using a mechanical latching mechanism rather than requiring continuous coil power. In this arrangement, the switch includes pole contacts that are moved between open and closed positions by a magnetic actuator, such as a coil-driven plunger. Once the desired position is reached, a latching structure keeps the contacts in place until the next switching operation.

The latching mechanism may include a resilient or spring-biased lock pin that travels along a defined guide path formed in or associated with a slider. The slider can include an indentation, cam path, groove, or similar shaped track that directs the movement of the lock pin during each actuation cycle. As the plunger or slider moves, the lock pin follows the track and is guided into a stable holding position. In one position, the mechanism holds the pole contacts in an engaged state, allowing current to pass through the switch. In another position, the mechanism holds the pole contacts in a disengaged state, interrupting the current path.

Because the latch maintains the switch position mechanically, the magnetic coil does not need to remain energized after switching is complete. Instead, the coil may be energized only briefly with a pulse of electrical power. This reduces power consumption, limits heat generation, and improves overall efficiency. The springy lock pin and shaped slider track also allow the latching function to be achieved with relatively low mechanical force, helping to reduce wear and improve switching reliability over repeated cycles.

The actuator may be driven by a coil rated for a particular voltage. When the coil receives a voltage pulse, it generates a magnetic field that pulls or drives the plunger, causing the contacts and latch mechanism to move. For lower-current switching applications, a lower-force actuation pulse may be sufficient. For higher-current switching, however, the pole contacts may require greater contact pressure, faster movement, or stronger mechanical force to overcome contact resistance, arcing effects, or heavier spring loading.

To support these higher-current applications, the design can allow a stronger coil operation by applying a higher-voltage discharge or pulse to the magnetic coil. The higher-voltage discharge increases the magnetic pull force available during actuation, enabling the plunger to move more decisively and ensuring reliable engagement or disengagement of the contacts. Since the pulse is brief, the coil can deliver increased actuation force without necessarily requiring continuous high-power operation.

This combination of a low-force mechanical latch and a selectively stronger magnetic actuation system provides a reliable and efficient switching structure. The latch securely maintains the relay or hybrid switch in its selected state, while the coil is used only when a transition between states is required. As a result, the switch can provide dependable contact retention, reduced steady-state energy use, and scalable performance for applications ranging from relatively light loads to higher-current electrical switching.

**Apparatus**

An apparatus is a set of tools, equipment, or devices designed to perform a specific task. It can be simple, such as a measuring instrument in a classroom, or complex, such as machinery used in a factory or laboratory. The word is often used in science, technology, medicine, and industry to describe equipment that supports work, research, or production.

In a laboratory, an apparatus may include glassware, burners, microscopes, sensors, and other instruments needed to carry out experiments. In medicine, an apparatus might refer to equipment used for diagnosis, treatment, or patient support, such as a breathing apparatus or imaging machine. In engineering, apparatus can include mechanical or electrical systems that help complete specialized operations.

The importance of an apparatus lies in its ability to make tasks easier, safer, more accurate, and more efficient. Proper use and maintenance are essential because damaged or poorly handled equipment can lead to incorrect results or dangerous situations. For this reason, users must understand how an apparatus works and follow safety instructions carefully.

Overall, an apparatus is a practical and essential part of many fields. Whether used for learning, research, healthcare, or manufacturing, it helps people perform tasks that would otherwise be difficult or impossible.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract for an apparatus and method involving a mechanically latched relay or hybrid switch using a springy lock pin, slider indentation path, and magnetic coil pulse operation.
counterfactuals.output: An apparatus and method are disclosed for operating a mechanically latched electrical switching device, such as a relay or hybrid switch. The device includes a movable contact actuator driven by at least one magnetic coil pulse and a mechanical latch assembly configured to retain the actuator in a selected switching state without continuous coil energization. The latch assembly includes a resilient lock pin biased into engagement with a slider having an indentation path formed therein. During actuation, a magnetic pulse displaces the slider or actuator along the indentation path, causing the springy lock pin to ride over a guide surface and seat within a locking recess to hold the switch in an open or closed state. A subsequent coil pulse moves the slider to release the lock pin from the recess and permit transition to an alternate state. The indentation path may include cam, ramp, detent, or dwell regions to define stable latched positions and controlled release motion. In hybrid embodiments, the mechanical contacts cooperate with a semiconductor switching element to reduce arcing during make or break operations. The arrangement provides low-power bistable switching, improved resistance to vibration-induced release, and simplified pulse-controlled actuation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a legalistic technical description of a mechanical latching device for one pole of a relay or hybrid switch, maintaining contact state with a springy lock pin, guided slider, and enhanced magnetic coil drive.
counterfactuals.output:
A mechanical latching device is provided for one pole of an electromechanical relay, contactor, hybrid switch, or similar switching apparatus, the device being configured to maintain a selected contact state without continuous energization of an actuator coil. The latching device comprises a movable contact carrier associated with a pole of the switch, a guided slider mechanically coupled directly or indirectly to the movable contact carrier, a resilient locking member in the form of a springy lock pin, and an electromagnetic drive arrangement including an enhanced magnetic coil assembly for selectively displacing the slider between at least two stable operating positions.

The movable contact carrier is arranged to carry or actuate a movable contact element relative to a corresponding stationary contact element. In a first operating position, the movable contact element is held in engagement with the stationary contact element, thereby defining a closed contact state of the pole. In a second operating position, the movable contact element is held spaced from the stationary contact element, thereby defining an open contact state of the pole. The latching device is configured such that at least one of the first and second operating positions is retained mechanically by the springy lock pin, independently of continued electrical energization of the magnetic coil assembly.

The guided slider is received in a guide structure, which may be formed by a housing, frame, molded carrier, pole module, or other support member of the relay or hybrid switch. The guide structure defines a substantially linear displacement path for the slider, although arcuate or compound guided motion may alternatively be used. The slider includes at least one locking formation, such as a recess, notch, shoulder, groove, cam surface, detent pocket, aperture, or stepped profile, configured to cooperate with the springy lock pin. The slider may further include an actuator-engagement portion arranged to receive force from an armature, plunger, yoke, magnetic core, or other movable magnetic element driven by the coil assembly.

The springy lock pin is mounted relative to the guide structure so as to be elastically deflectable transverse to the displacement direction of the slider. The lock pin may be formed as a bent wire, leaf-spring pin, resilient rod, spring-biased pin, torsionally loaded latch finger, or integrally formed resilient projection. The lock pin is biased toward the slider and is positioned to enter or bear against the locking formation of the slider when the slider reaches a predetermined latching position. Engagement of the lock pin with the locking formation prevents unintended reverse movement of the slider and thereby maintains the associated contact state of the pole. The resilience of the lock pin permits the pin to deflect during intentional switching movement, allowing the slider to pass over or through a cammed portion of the locking formation until the pin snaps or settles into a stable retaining position.

The slider and lock pin are preferably configured such that a relatively low holding force is required to maintain the contact state after latching, while a higher threshold force is required to release the latch. This threshold force may be selected by the geometry of the locking formation, the spring constant of the lock pin, the inclination of the cam surfaces, the coefficient of friction between the engaging members, and the direction of force applied by the electromagnetic drive. In one embodiment, the locking formation includes a ramp surface for deflecting the springy lock pin during movement into the latched position and a retaining shoulder for resisting return movement. In another embodiment, opposed ramp surfaces are provided to permit bistable latching in both the open and closed contact states.

The enhanced magnetic coil drive comprises a coil, a magnetic core, and a movable magnetic member arranged to generate an impulse or stroke sufficient to displace the guided slider from one latched position to another. The magnetic coil drive may include a magnetic flux concentrator, pole shoe, low-reluctance yoke, permanent-magnet biasing element, dual-winding coil, pulse-drive winding, magnetic shunt, or overtravel compensation feature to increase available actuation force or improve switching reliability. The coil drive is preferably configured for pulsed operation, such that electrical power is applied only during transition between contact states. Upon completion of the transition, the springy lock pin retains the slider in the selected position and the coil may be de-energized.

In a preferred configuration, the coil drive includes a movable armature coupled to the slider through a lost-motion connection, impact surface, toggle link, or direct abutment. The armature is accelerated by the magnetic field generated upon energization of the coil and transfers mechanical energy to the slider. The transferred energy causes the slider to overcome the locking resistance of the springy lock pin, thereby releasing the slider from a first detent position and driving it toward a second detent position. When the slider reaches the second position, the lock pin elastically engages a corresponding locking formation and mechanically secures the slider against unintended displacement.

The latching device may be arranged so that the springy lock pin retains the contacts in a normally open state, a normally closed state, or both. Where used in a hybrid switch, the latching device may cooperate with semiconductor switching elements, arc-suppression circuitry, or contact commutation circuitry. For example, the mechanical pole may be closed after a semiconductor device has initially conducted current, or opened after current has been commutated away from the mechanical contacts, thereby reducing arcing and contact wear. The mechanical latch maintains the physical contact state after the switching event, reducing standby power consumption and thermal loading of the coil.

The guided slider may further include position-indicating features, auxiliary-contact actuation surfaces, reset surfaces, damping surfaces, or end-stop engagement portions. One or more springs may be provided to bias the movable contact carrier, the slider, or the armature toward a selected direction. The springy lock pin may serve solely as a retaining latch or may additionally provide part of the contact force, return force, or tactile detent force of the mechanism.

The components are preferably arranged such that mechanical tolerances, vibration, shock, and contact bounce do not cause inadvertent unlatching. To this end, the retaining shoulder of the locking formation may be oriented so that contact reaction forces tend to seat the lock pin more firmly in the locking formation. The guide structure may constrain the slider against lateral displacement and may include bearing surfaces, ribs, slots, rails, or channels to reduce friction and maintain alignment between the slider and the lock pin. The lock pin may be retained in opposed supports or molded pockets to ensure repeatable spring deflection and to avoid plastic deformation during repeated switching cycles.

In operation, energization of the enhanced magnetic coil drive in a first polarity, winding, or pulse condition produces movement of the armature and drives the slider from the open-contact position toward the closed-contact position. During this movement, the springy lock pin is cammed out of a first locking formation or detent and subsequently enters a second locking formation corresponding to the closed-contact position. The movable contact carrier is thereby positioned so that the movable contact engages the stationary contact. After the coil drive is de-energized, the closed-contact state remains mechanically maintained by the engagement between the springy lock pin and the second locking formation.

To open the pole, the coil drive is energized in a second polarity, winding, or pulse condition, or a separate release coil is energized, thereby applying a release force to the slider or armature. The release force causes the slider to overcome the retaining force of the springy lock pin. The lock pin deflects elastically out of the closed-position locking formation, permitting the slider to move toward the open-contact position. When the slider reaches the open-contact position, the lock pin engages the first locking formation and mechanically retains the slider in the open-contact state after removal of coil power.

The described latching device thereby provides a compact, low-power, mechanically stable retention arrangement for one pole of a relay or hybrid switching apparatus. The combination of the guided slider, resilient lock pin, and enhanced magnetic coil drive permits reliable state change under pulsed actuation while maintaining the selected contact state without continuous coil energization. The structure is suitable for modular pole construction and may be implemented in single-pole or multi-pole devices, with each pole having an independent latching device or with multiple poles actuated by a common magnetic drive.
